response:
Serverless ML inference platforms (Lambda, Cloud Run, modal, Fly Machines, etc.) spin up containers on-demand, and the cold-start penalty — the latency between request arrival and first token — is not uniform across quantization schemes. The central question is: why does a 4-bit GPTQ model cold-start slower than its fp16 counterpart on the same hardware, even though it's smaller on disk? The answer lies in the asymmetry between storage size (what gets loaded from object storage or image layers) and runtime memory construction cost (dequantization kernel initialization, weight unpacking, calibration data rehydration, and CUDA graph capture), which beginners collapse into a single "model size" variable.

An expert worries specifically about kernel warmup asymmetry: quantized models like AWQ or GPTQ require custom CUDA kernels (e.g., ExLlamaV2, Marlin) that aren't compiled ahead-of-time in standard container images, so JIT compilation hits during cold-start, not during serving — a cost invisible in steady-state benchmarks. A second expert concern is memory bandwidth saturation during weight staging: on serverless hardware with shared, throttled NVMe or network-attached storage, loading a 4-bit model that immediately dequantizes to fp16 in VRAM can consume more peak bandwidth than simply loading fp16 weights directly, because the dequant is compute-bound and stalls the I/O pipeline rather than overlapping with it. Beginners look at checkpoint file size and predict cold-start time linearly; experts look at the full chain from bytes-on-disk through kernel init through first-batch CUDA graph capture and know the bottleneck migrates depending on quantization regime, hardware tier, and whether the runtime uses eager vs. compiled execution.

A Marlin-kernel GPTQ cold-start breaks into roughly five sequential phases: (1) container/VM provisioning (50–400ms depending on platform; Modal with pre-warmed microVMs sits at the low end, Cloud Run closer to 400ms), (2) model weight fetch from object storage or image layer (proportional to checkpoint size — a 4-bit Llama-3 70B is ~35GB, so at typical 2–4 GB/s NVMe throughput that's 9–18 seconds, but network-attached storage on burst-credit exhaustion can hit 500 MB/s, tripling this), (3) CUDA context initialization (~200–800ms, hardware and driver-version dependent), (4) Marlin kernel load and weight repacking — this is the asymmetric phase: Marlin requires converting GPTQ-packed int4 weights into its own tile layout in VRAM, which for a 70B model runs 8–15 seconds on an A100 and cannot be parallelized across the weight fetch, and (5) CUDA graph capture for the static decode graph (~1–4 seconds depending on sequence length and batch size). The variance across 100 cold-starts comes overwhelmingly from phases 2 and 4: phase 2 varies because serverless storage I/O is multiplexed and burst credits are shared across tenants, producing a bimodal distribution (fast-path cache hit vs. cold object fetch); phase 4 varies because the Marlin repacking is sensitive to VRAM fragmentation state and PCIe bandwidth contention from concurrent tenants on the same physical host. Crucially, profiling tools like nsys or PyTorch's torch.profiler only capture from CUDA context initialization onward, so phases 1–2 are typically invisible in the traces researchers publish, causing systematic underreporting of true P99 cold-start latency in papers like the vLLM and TensorRT-LLM benchmarks. A practical consequence: the Marlin paper reports repacking overhead in isolation on dedicated hardware, but in serverless the repacking and storage fetch are often serialized rather than overlapped, so the real cold-start is super-additive relative to what you'd predict from either number alone.

Storing the post-repack Marlin layout directly solves phase 4 but creates three concrete problems that explain why platforms avoid it. First, portability collapse: Marlin's tile layout is specific to SM80/SM86/SM89 warp geometry (the A100/A10G/RTX 4090 family); the same repacked weights are invalid on H100 (SM90, which uses a different wgmma instruction layout) or any AMD target, so a platform serving heterogeneous GPU fleets — which all major providers do for cost and availability reasons — would need to store N layout variants per model, multiplying storage costs and complicating routing logic. Second, storage inflation: GPTQ int4 packs 8 weights per 32-bit word; Marlin's tile layout adds padding and metadata for its 2D warp-tile structure, expanding the checkpoint by roughly 10–15% — not catastrophic for one model, but at platform scale (Modal, Replicate, and Baseten each host thousands of model variants) this compounds into meaningful object storage costs and, more importantly, increases the phase 2 fetch time slightly, partially eroding the phase 4 savings. Third, kernel versioning entanglement: the repacked layout is tightly coupled to the exact Marlin kernel version (and by extension the vLLM or SGLang commit that ships it); when the kernel is updated for performance or correctness — which happened multiple times between vLLM 0.3 and 0.6 — stored repacked weights either become stale (silently producing wrong outputs if layout assumptions shift) or require invalidation and re-repack, creating a cache coherence problem that GPTQ-format weights don't have since they're a stable interchange format. What platforms actually do instead is a middle path: CUDA graph caching and kernel pre-compilation (Modal's @app.cls with @modal.build(), Baseten's engine caching) which saves phases 3 and 5 across warm restarts but leaves the repack cost in place; the repack is treated as acceptable because it's more reproducible and hardware-agnostic than layout serialization.

response:
CUDA graph capture requires static tensor shapes at record time, so serving variable sequence lengths or batch sizes naively means either capturing a separate graph per (batch_size, seq_len) pair or falling back to eager execution — and for quantized models the problem is sharper because Marlin and AWQ kernels have their own shape constraints on top of the attention shapes. vLLM's solution is to capture a discrete set of graphs at a fixed batch size ladder (typically powers of two: 1, 2, 4, 8, ... up to max_batch) and a fixed maximum sequence length, padding inputs to the nearest ladder rung at runtime; for a 4-bit Llama-3 70B on A100 this means capturing ~12–16 graphs, each taking 1–3 seconds, so phase 5 alone runs 20–40 seconds during cold-start, and this is documented but rarely highlighted in vLLM's own benchmarks. TensorRT-LLM takes a more aggressive approach with its "inflight batching" engine: it uses a separate CUDA graph per beam configuration and relies on TRT's engine optimization to pre-compile multiple profiles (specified at engine build time via --opt_batch_size flags), which shifts the capture cost entirely offline — but this means the serialized engine is model+hardware+batch-profile specific, reinforcing the portability problem from the previous question and making engine reuse across GPU generations impossible. SGLang's RadixAttention partially sidesteps this by using a chunked prefill strategy where the graph is captured for fixed chunk sizes rather than full sequence lengths, reducing the combinatorial capture space substantially, though their 2024 paper shows this introduces ~5–8% throughput regression versus full-sequence graphs on decode-heavy workloads. The correctness risk that experts watch for is graph capture with incorrect quantization state: if the Marlin weight pointer or scale tensor is captured into the graph before the repack is fully flushed (a race condition possible when repack runs async to overlap with graph capture initiation), the graph replays with a stale memory address — this produces silent numerical errors rather than crashes, and it's the kind of bug that appears only at P99 cold-starts under memory pressure, not in unit tests.

Warm pooling sounds like a clean solution but quantized models create a specific economic inversion that doesn't exist for fp16: the whole point of quantization is to fit more model into less VRAM, but a warm pool pins that VRAM whether or not requests are arriving, so you pay the GPU cost continuously while capturing none of the multiplexing benefit that makes quantization attractive in the first place. For fp16 models, warm pooling is straightforward because the runtime state is essentially just the weights in VRAM plus a CUDA context — if you need to serve multiple model variants, you can time-share one GPU across warm fp16 instances by swapping weights through host memory (a technique Modal and Replicate both use with NVLink or pinned host memory as a staging buffer). Quantized models break this weight-swapping approach because the Marlin-repacked layout is significantly harder to partially evict and reload than fp16 weights: fp16 tensors can be swapped layer-by-layer with minimal reinitialization, but Marlin's tile structure couples adjacent weight blocks in a way that makes partial eviction semantically invalid without a full repack on reload, meaning you can't do the incremental swap-in that makes fp16 time-sharing work. The economics shift adversarially at low request rates: a warm fp16 70B instance on a single A100 ($2.50–3.50/hr on Lambda or CoreWeave) can be time-shared across 3–4 model variants with acceptable swap latency (~2–4s), but a warm 4-bit 70B instance occupies roughly 35GB of a 80GB A100 and cannot easily share that VRAM with other repacked models, so you're paying for dedicated VRAM that's idle most of the time — the quantization VRAM savings accrue to the provider's bin-packing, not to the customer's cost structure. Modal's actual warm pool implementation (their keep_warm=N parameter) sidesteps this by keeping entire container+GPU pairs alive, which works but means the customer pays full GPU-seconds for idle warm instances — for a low-traffic endpoint serving a 4-bit model, the warm pool cost can exceed the inference cost by 10-100x depending on request rate. The deeper problem is that the quantization benefit was always about throughput density (more concurrent requests per GPU) not latency for a single idle instance, and warm pooling for low-traffic endpoints selects precisely the regime where throughput density provides zero value.

response:
Streaming weight loading — starting inference on early transformer layers while later layers are still fetching — is architecturally natural for decoder-only models since layer 0 must complete before layer 1 regardless, but quantized models introduce a specific sequencing violation: the scale and zero-point tensors for each GPTQ layer are stored interleaved with or adjacent to the weight shards in HuggingFace's safetensors layout, but Marlin's repack needs the full layer's weight tensor contiguous in memory before it can tile it, meaning you can't begin repacking layer N until the entire layer N weight block has landed, which for a 70B model means each layer's ~800MB shard must fully arrive before any useful GPU work begins on that layer. The safetensors format actually makes streaming more tractable than the older pytorch .bin format because its header encodes byte offsets for every tensor, enabling direct seeking — and this is the basis for HuggingFace's safetensors streaming loader — but the Marlin repack requirement means the practical pipeline is fetch-full-layer → repack → next-layer, with no overlap between storage I/O and GPU compute, whereas fp16 models can begin attention computation on layer 0 tokens while layer 1 weights are still loading. The one production system that has done something close to this is Apple's MLX framework for Apple Silicon, which exploits unified memory to begin computation on partially-loaded weight pages using the Metal GPU scheduler — but this works because Apple Silicon has no PCIe boundary between storage DMA and GPU, a hardware property that doesn't exist on any datacenter GPU where weights must cross PCIe from host DRAM to VRAM as a discrete transfer. Nvidia's CUDA 12.2 introduced cuMemMap with cudaMemPrefetchAsync which theoretically allows overlapping PCIe transfer with compute on already-arrived pages, and there are research prototypes (notably from the OSDI 2024 context around Splitwise and DistServe) that exploit this for fp16 prefill/decode disaggregation, but nobody has shipped this for quantized models in production because the Marlin repack sits between the PCIe transfer and the compute and breaks the pipeline. The fundamental obstacle is that streaming weight loading requires the compute graph to be expressible as a function of a prefix of the weights, which is true for fp16 transformers (each layer is self-contained) but becomes false for quantized models whose kernels require whole-layer weight tiles — making this a kernel design problem as much as a systems problem, and one that would require Marlin-style kernels to be redesigned to accept partial tile loads, which hasn't happened because the steady-state throughput optimization (full tile, maximum tensorcore utilization) points in exactly the opposite direction.

The tension here is fundamental: Marlin achieves its throughput (near-theoretical peak of ~3.9 TB/s effective memory bandwidth on A100) precisely because its tile geometry is large enough to fully saturate warp-level tensorcore pipelines, and decomposing into smaller independently-computable units shrinks the tile below the threshold where the dequantization arithmetic can be hidden behind memory latency — you fall off the efficiency cliff that separates Marlin from naive int4 kernels. The most credible candidate for streaming-compatible quantized inference is GGUF/llama.cpp's row-quantization format (Q4_K_M and variants), where each row of the weight matrix is independently quantized with its own scale and min values stored contiguously with the row's weights in a fixed 256-element block — this means any individual block is self-contained and can be dequantized and multiplied independently, enabling genuine streaming at block granularity (~1KB units), but the cost is that llama.cpp's CUDA kernels achieve roughly 60–70% of Marlin's throughput on the same hardware because the smaller tile size prevents full tensorcore saturation. FlashInfer's recent work on block-sparse quantization (their 2024 preprint) points toward a middle path: using 128×128 weight tiles that are large enough for efficient tensorcore use but stored with self-contained metadata, which would reduce the streaming granularity from "full layer" (~800MB) to "tile" (~64KB) — still not byte-level streaming but enough to begin GPU compute after ~1% of a layer has arrived rather than 100%. The architectural sacrifice you can't avoid is scale tensor locality: any scheme where each small unit carries its own quantization parameters inflates the metadata overhead (scales and zeros go from ~0.5% of weight size in GPTQ to ~3–6% in fine-grained per-block schemes) and more importantly reintroduces the accuracy degradation that group quantization with large group sizes (128 or 256) was designed to avoid — smaller groups mean more scales mean more metadata bandwidth pressure means you've partially negated the memory bandwidth savings that motivated 4-bit quantization. What nobody has built but the math supports is a hierarchical tile format: coarse outer tiles (128×512, large enough for Marlin-class tensorcore efficiency) with inner 64×64 sub-tiles that are independently dequantizable, stored in an order that allows sub-tile streaming while preserving outer-tile compute efficiency — the obstacle is that this requires a new kernel that simultaneously handles two levels of tiling, which is a significant CUDA engineering investment with no obvious academic publication incentive since the benefit only materializes in the serverless cold-start regime, not in the steady-state benchmarks that drive kernel development.

response:
The idea is genuinely attractive and maps onto a real pattern in systems design — adaptive bitrate streaming in video (HLS/DASH switching codec profiles based on bandwidth) does exactly this — but ML inference has three specific properties that make runtime format switching much harder than it looks. The first is the accuracy discontinuity: GPTQ calibration is not format-agnostic; a model quantized with group-size-128 for Marlin efficiency and a model quantized with group-size-32 for streaming granularity are different quantized models with different weight values and different perplexity characteristics (typically 0.3–0.8 perplexity points difference on Wikitext-2 for Llama-class models), so switching formats mid-serving means switching to a model with detectably different output distributions — for stateless single-turn inference this might be acceptable, but for multi-turn sessions it introduces response consistency violations that are user-visible. The second is the switching latency itself: transitioning from fine-grained GGUF-style serving to Marlin-layout serving requires evicting the current weight layout from VRAM, fetching or recomputing the Marlin-repacked layout, and recapturing CUDA graphs — on a 70B model this is a 30–60 second dead zone during which the endpoint is unavailable, meaning the traffic spike that triggers the switch is exactly the traffic you fail to serve during the switch, which is worse than staying in the suboptimal format. The third obstacle is state entanglement in the KV cache: any in-flight requests have KV cache entries computed under the fine-grained quantization's weight values; after switching to coarse quantization, continuing those sequences produces attention outputs that are subtly inconsistent with the prefill, and draining all in-flight requests before switching adds queuing delay that compounds the switchover dead zone. The closest production analog is Ollama's dynamic model loading, which does swap between GGUF quantization levels (Q4_K_M vs Q8_0) based on available VRAM, but it does this only at cold-load time with zero in-flight requests and explicitly accepts the accuracy difference as a user-configured tradeoff rather than a transparent runtime decision. What would make this feasible is if the two quantization formats shared identical weight values and differed only in layout — which is theoretically possible if you designed a master format that can be re-tiled without requantization — but current GPTQ and GGUF quantization pipelines bake format assumptions into the calibration step, coupling accuracy to layout in a way that would require a clean-room redesign of the quantization toolchain to separate.
